analysis.one_liner: Forces pharmacy benefit managers to pay pharmacies their real costs and pass drug rebates to patients in Medicare and Medicaid.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to restrict pharmacy benefit managers in Medicare and Medicaid was introduced with 41 cosponsors (25 Republicans, 16 Democrats) and sent to two House committees, where no action has been scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the rules for pharmacy benefit managers — the middleman companies that stand between drug plans and pharmacies for most Americans' prescriptions. It would require PBMs and drug plans in Medicare and Medicaid to pay pharmacies based on the actual national average cost of a drug plus a modest fee, pass manufacturer rebates to patients at the pharmacy counter instead of pocketing them, and stop practices that steer patients to PBM-owned pharmacies. It adds criminal penalties of up to $1 million in fines and 10 years in prison for knowingly violating the payment rules, and it expands price-survey reporting in Medicaid to cover mail-order, specialty, and hospital pharmacies.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare Part D enrollees and Medicaid beneficiaries, who would see manufacturer rebates applied directly to their copays at the pharmacy counter rather than being applied later or absorbed by intermediaries. Independent and community pharmacies would gain guaranteed reimbursement at the national average drug acquisition cost plus a dispensing fee, instead of opaque rates that can be below their purchase price. Patients would also keep the right to use any in-network pharmacy without being pushed toward PBM-affiliated stores.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare and Medicaid patients, community pharmacies

how_it_helps.text: Requires Medicare Part D plans and PBMs to reimburse in-network pharmacies at the national average drug acquisition cost on the day of the claim (or wholesale acquisition cost if no survey price exists), plus a fee of 4% of that cost or $50, whichever is less, and a dispensing fee matching the state Medicaid rate [S2].
Requires manufacturer rebates on Part D drugs to be applied at the point of sale, reducing the patient's copay or coinsurance, and requires PBMs to remit full rebate amounts to the plan sponsor [S2].

Prohibits steering — practices that push enrollees to use a PBM-affiliated pharmacy, including preferred or narrow networks that exclude independent pharmacies or raise patient costs when they don't switch [S2].

Imposes criminal penalties of up to a $1 million fine and 10 years in prison, and civil monetary penalties, on PBMs that knowingly and willfully violate the payment rules, rebate pass-through rules, or steering ban [S2].
Applies the same payment and rebate rules to Medicaid managed care contracts and requires that all manufacturer rebates received under Medicaid be remitted to the state [S2].

Expands the Medicaid drug price survey to cover mail-order, specialty, nursing home, hospital, and clinic pharmacies — not just retail community pharmacies — and requires the government to publish national drug acquisition prices and information on price concessions [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Pharmacy benefit managers would lose the margin between what plans pay them and what they pay pharmacies (spread pricing), rebate revenue they currently retain, and the steering advantage their own pharmacies enjoy. Insurers operating PBM subsidiaries would face the same exposure. If guaranteed pharmacy payment raises plan costs, part of the expense could surface in higher Medicare premiums or federal subsidy costs, and plans could respond by narrowing pharmacy networks.
analysis.who_pays_short: Pharmacy benefit managers and their corporate owners

drawbacks.text: Guaranteeing pharmacies cost-based reimbursement plus a dispensing fee raises plan drug costs, which could push up Medicare premiums, federal subsidy spending, or Medicaid costs for states unless offset elsewhere [S2].
The bill does not include an offset or funding mechanism in its text, so it would increase federal mandatory spending on its own under current scoring conventions [S2].

Plans might respond to higher pharmacy payment obligations by cutting the number of pharmacies they contract with, which could reduce convenience for patients in rural areas even as payment per prescription improves [S2].

The strict definition of steering — including any multi-tier network or accreditation standard that differentially treats pharmacies — is broad enough that plans argue it could prevent legitimate tools for managing costs, a trade-off supporters accept to protect pharmacy access [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients, the most direct gains are lower copays at the counter from point-of-sale rebates and better pharmacy payment that keeps community pharmacies open — a real problem in rural areas where store closures have left people driving long distances. The honest cost is that paying pharmacies more and guaranteeing rebate pass-through raises plan drug costs, which ultimately shows up in premiums or federal and state budgets. The bill deliberately chooses pharmacy access and transparent pricing over the current system's lower paper costs, and it backs the rules with criminal penalties — a serious enforcement tool aimed squarely at three dominant middleman companies.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was just introduced and referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees, where it is waiting for a hearing or markup that has not been scheduled.

narrative.text: Rep. Jake Auchincloss (D-MA) introduced the Pharmacists Fight Back in Medicare and Medicaid Act on December 11, 2025, joined by a bipartisan group of original cosponsors including Republicans Diana Harshbarger and James Comer [S1][S2].
The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and, in addition, to the Ways and Means Committee, with no further action recorded since introduction [S4].
The bill has 41 cosponsors, 25 Republicans and 16 Democrats [S3].
The bill's provisions would take effect for plan years beginning on or after January 1, 2027, with penalties applying beginning on that date [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmacy benefit managers remain unregulated under these rules, and their revenue model is untouched for now.

sides.party_line_note: Support is split almost evenly across parties — 25 Republican and 16 Democratic cosponsors — with the sponsor a Democrat and the top two original cosponsor Republicans.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers (CVS Caremark, Express Scripts, Optum Rx)
industries.note: The bill bans the core of the PBM business model in Medicare and Medicaid: spread pricing (paying pharmacies less than the plan pays the PBM), rebate retention, and steering patients to PBM-owned pharmacies, backed by criminal penalties. PBMs profit by taking a cut between what plans pay and what pharmacies receive, which runs directly against patients and pharmacies.

Pharmacies would be guaranteed reimbursement at the national average acquisition cost plus a fee and dispensing payment, ending arrangements that can pay them below their own purchase price. Their interest in staying solvent runs alongside patients' interest in having a pharmacy nearby.

The steering ban removes the structural advantage that funnels patients to pharmacies owned by PBM parent companies, while payment floors would raise per-prescription revenue for all pharmacies including affiliated ones.

industries.industry: Medicare Part D insurers and Medicaid managed care plans
industries.note: Plans face guaranteed higher pharmacy payment costs and loss of rebate margins, which could raise premiums or cut into plan profits, but plans are also banned from steering and rebate games played through PBM affiliates.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in two committees with no hearing or markup scheduled. Bipartisan PBM bills have repeatedly surfaced in Congress, and some narrower PBM provisions have advanced in larger packages, but standalone bills like this one rarely move without leadership scheduling. The most realistic path is that it stalls unless PBM regulation gets attached to a broader health or drug pricing bill late in the session.
